newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Dec 4.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-PRESS DIGEST-Australian General News - Dec 4.

text.p: (Compiled for Reuters by Media Monitors)
THE AUSTRALIAN FINANCIAL REVIEW

Communications Minister Richard Alston last night unveiled the Federal Government's new telecommunications competition package. The package will see Australia's telecommunications industry open up to be one of the most liberal in the world, with no limit on the number of carriers and the introduction of a new competition framework to be administered by the Australian Competition and Consumer Commission. The package will end the duopoly of Telstra and Optus and will be introduced on July 1, 1997. Page 1.

Telecommunications Industry Ombudsman John Pinnock warned yesterday that as the price of mobile phones continues to fall, and an expected one in four Australians will own one, buyers must be aware that the purchase of their phone does not include a raft of extra charges. Page 1.

After considering a submission from Resources Minister Warwick Parer and Primary Industries and Energy Minister John Anderson relating to multiple land use in areas reserved under the new regional forest agreements (RFAs), Federal Cabinet has deferred a dcision to allow mining and mineral exploration in these areas because of fears it may derail the new national reserves system. Page 2.

Private forecaster Access Economics warned last night the Commonwealth's fiscal tightening was already being undermined by looser policy in the States. It claimed that for each dollar saved by the Federal Government, State Governments have since spent a ollar, mainly on capital spending. The warning came as Budget measures to reduce higher education funding were stalled in the Senate. Page 2.
THE AUSTRALIAN

Prime Minister John Howard and Deputy Prime Minister Tim Fischer were at odds over the impact of the high Australian dollar yesterday. Fischer questioned whether the currency had risen too far and was damaging exports, while Howard said the rising dollar was an aid to business, although he recognised there were some "minuses" as well as benefits. Page 1.

The Speaker of the House of Representatives, Bob Halverson, was forced to review a ruling yesterday after Industrial Relations Minister Peter Reith twice refused to withdraw a remark deemed as offensive and Prime Minister John Howard stated he was at "a complete loss" to understand the ruling. Returning to Parliament four hours later, Halverson said no offensive remark had been made by Reith. Page 1.

Rod Dent, the son of the first man to die under the Northern Territory's euthanasia legislation, has withdrawn his support for the laws and his backing Federal legislation to overturn them. Dent came to his decision after watching a video of his father in 1992 and coming to the conclusion that he had resorted to euthanasia because he was "very depressed" about the state of palliative care in the medical system. Page 1.

The preliminary results of a 20-year study into women's health in Australia has revealed that more than half of young women hope to juggle a full-time career and a family by the age of 35 and more than one in two older women experience no limitations in their daily activities. The study also found that while women are gaining weight in general, one in four young women are underweight. Page 1.
THE SYDNEY MORNING HERALD

Australia's 90,000 Hong Kong immigrants granted residency visas in the first six years of this decade will be among those affected by China's call for all emigrants to return to Hong Kong by June 30, 1997 to qualify for residency. Prime Minister John Howard will talk to Hong Kong's leading democratic politician, Martin Lee, when he attends a reception Howard is hosting for delegates to a conference of the International Democrat Union. Page 1.

The first instalment of data from the Australian Longitudinal Study on Women's Health by the Universities of Newcastle and Queensland has highlighted major concerns in women's health, including body weight and menstruation related problems. The study found that more than a quarter of women aged 18-22 were underweight and 22 per cent of mid-life women had had a hysterectomy, while 17 per cent reported pre-menstrual tension. Page 1.

As the Government complains that the Senate's blocking of spending cuts could stop interest rates falling or force the lifting of taxes, it announced yesterday that small business would receive a boost from changes to capital gains tax. Treasurer Peter Cstello said the reforms were consistent with the Government's election mandate and will cost A$200 million when they come into effect on July 1 next year. Page 1.

Announcing he had reversed his support for the Northern Territory's euthanasia legislation, under which his father was the first person to die, Rod Dent admitted to a press conference yesterday that he now backed the Federal bill to overturn the euthanasia legislation in hope of political advancement in the New South Wales Liberal Party. Page 1.
THE AGE

The Victorian branch of the Australian Medical Association and the Victorian Council for Civil Liberties yesterday attacked a State Government plan to allow police to take blood and urine samples from motorists suspected of drug use. A parliamentary roadsafety committee report tabled in the Victorian Parliament yesterday recommended police be given the power to force drivers to undergo a roadside impairment test and if necessary a more detailed follow-up assessment. If the driver failed the second test, police would be free to seek a blood or urine sample. Page A1.

Family Court head Justice Alastair Nicholson has warned new legal aid guidelines passed down by the Victorian Family Court could lead to a risk in children's welfare. Nicholson believes the guidelines breach a United Nations convention that seeks to protct the rights of children and that child sexual assault cases could be threatened by a A$15,000 cap on funds spent on separate legal representation for children. Page A1.

A two-year price freeze on Public Transport Corporation fares will cease from 1 January, with casual commuters paying 20 cents more for a daily zone one ticket, at A$4.30, and two-hour zone one fares rising by 10 cents to A$2.20. Weekly and monthly ticket holders will face only a two per cent rise in fares. Page A1.

Victorian Opposition Leader John Brumby has claimed in Parliament that a senior Treasury official said the attitude of the Department of the Premier and Cabinet to the review of the office of Victorian auditor-general Ches Baragwanath was "If this doesn't stick you up, nothing will." Brumby says the statement explains the true motivations behind the review. Page A3.
-- Reuters Sydney Newsroom 61-2 9373-1800
